title: Baptism, deeper
hook: some say baptism brings new birth; others that it signs a birth already happened

segments.voice: Yesterday, the priesthood of all believers, from the altar to the cobbler's bench. Your line was a royal priesthood. Which ordinary task did you do heartily, and for whom? Day one thousand one hundred.

It's night, and a respected teacher named Nicodemus has come to find Jesus quietly. He opens politely. Jesus skips the politeness and says a man must be born again to see the kingdom of God. Nicodemus is baffled, and says so: "How can a man be born when he is old?" Climb back into your mother? Jesus answers with two elements: water and Spirit. Since then, water has been poured over infants at stone fonts, and grown adults have gone under in rivers. And Christians have read his answer in more than one way. Today's word, taken deeper: baptism.
screen: `HOW CAN A MAN BE BORN WHEN OLD?`

segments.voice: Here's the answer, in the King James: "Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God." Born of water. Churches across the traditions baptize. The question underneath is what the water does. One answer: baptism is God's own act, and in it God gives the new birth. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Anglican teaching point to Paul's phrase in his letter to Titus, "the washing of regeneration," and read it as describing the font itself. That's one reason these churches baptize infants. A baby can't decide anything, and in their teaching that's the point: the gift comes first, before anyone can earn it. Faith is meant to grow up inside the gift. A second answer: baptism is an outward sign of a new birth God gives by the Spirit through faith. Baptist churches and other believers' churches teach that a person is born again by trusting Christ, and then baptized, usually by full immersion, as a public witness that it has already happened. So they baptize those old enough to say so for themselves. Presbyterian and Reformed churches take a third road: they baptize the infants of believers as a sign and seal of God's covenant promise, while teaching that the water doesn't work automatically. Now look at what they share. Paul, writing to the Romans: "we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life." Under the water, a burial. Out of the water, a rising. Whether the new birth happens in that moment or is shown by it, these readings keep the same shape: going down, and coming up, new.
screen: `BORN OF WATER AND OF THE SPIRIT.` · `GOD'S ACT: THE WASHING OF REGENERATION.` · `A SIGN OF A BIRTH ALREADY GIVEN.` · `A COVENANT SIGN AND SEAL.` · then, large: `BURIED WITH HIM, RAISED TO NEW LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember your baptism, or your beginning. Settle, and breathe slowly, as if surfacing from water. If you were baptized, bring it to mind, even if you only know it from a photo or a story: who was there, what was said, what the water was like. If you weren't, bring to mind a beginning that mattered to you, a moment you went under in some way and came up different. Notice what in it was given to you, and what you chose. If you pray, you can give thanks for that beginning. If you don't, just rest in having begun. The bell holds the time.
Baptism. Being washed, buried and raised in water: for some churches the new birth itself, for others its sign.
Your line: born of water. Today, each time you wash your hands or face, let it remind you of a beginning. Day one thousand one hundred.

howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Methodist and Reformed churches baptize infants as well as adults, by pouring, sprinkling or immersion; Baptist and other believers' churches baptize people who profess faith, usually by full immersion.

options: "how can a man be born when he is old?"
fork.reveal: he asks the obvious question out loud, and Jesus answers: "born of water and of the Spirit."

original.note: Greek: to dip, to immerse, to wash — the verb behind "baptize."

trapdoor: what you thought: baptism is a naming ceremony with water.
what it means: a washing that churches understand either as God giving the new birth, or as the sign and seal of it, all pictured as dying and rising with Christ.
what a scholar hears: baptizo, to dip or wash. John 3:5 joins water and Spirit; Titus 3:5 speaks of the washing of regeneration.

notes: Positions described: baptismal regeneration (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican), believer's baptism as public witness (Baptist and other believers' churches), covenant sign and seal for infants of believers (Presbyterian/Reformed). Methodist teaching is mentioned only in howItsDone. Confirm fairness and that no side is ranked.
The voice says 'churches across the traditions baptize' rather than 'every church'; the Salvation Army and Quakers do not practice water baptism.
Myth item 'only one church baptizes infants' reveal lists churches; confirm.
Original: βαπτίζω glossed 'to dip, to immerse, to wash' (cf. Mark 7:4, Luke 11:38); confirm.
Hook: 'stone fonts' and 'waist-deep in rivers' are illustrative pictures; confirm.
